questions.knowledge_point: Finding Laplace Transforms of Step Functions
questions.problem:
Find $L{f(t)}$ for the piecewise function defined by 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<1 \\ -7,\, & 1\le t\le 3 \\ 0,\, & t>3.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

For the piecewise function 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t)={\begin{aligned}0\, & \text{for}\,\,t<1 \\ -7\, & \text{for}\,\,1\le t\le 3 \\ 0\, & \text{for}\,\,t>3\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}f(t)\text{d}t={\int }_{1}^{3}(-7){e}^{-st}\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We calculate this definite integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{1}^{3}(-7){e}^{-st}\text{d}t \\  & ={\frac{7}{s}{e}^{-st}|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{7}{s}({e}^{-3s}-{e}^{-s})\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
L{f(t)}=\frac{7}{s}({e}^{-3s}-{e}^{-s}).
$$

questions.problem: Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s)=L{f(t)}$ for $s>0,$ where $f(t)=u(5-t)$ and $u$ is the unit step function.$\,F(s)=L{f(t)}=$ {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the unit step function is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<0 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise function 

$$
\begin{aligned}u(5-t)={\begin{aligned}1,\, & t\le 5 \\ 0,\, & t>5\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }u(5-t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}1\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{5}^{\infty }0\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We compute this integral for $s>0$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{5}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{{e}^{-st}}{s}]}_{0}^{5} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-5s}}{s}+\frac{1}{s} \\  & =\frac{1}{s}(1-{e}^{-5s})\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s)=L{f(t)},$ where $f(t)$ is given by 

$$
f(t)={\begin{aligned}-1,\, & x\le 4 \\ 1\, & x>4\end{aligned}
$$

$\,F(s)=L{f(t)}=$ {{field-1}},
valid for {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise function 

$$
f(t)={\begin{aligned}-1,\, & x\le 4 \\ 1\, & x>4\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}(-1)\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{4}^{\infty }1\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{4}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{4}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the improper integral diverges if $s\le 0.$

For $s>0,$ we calculate our Laplace transform as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & =-{\int }_{0}^{4}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{4}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{s}{[{e}^{-st}]}_{0}^{4}+{\int }_{4}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-4s}}{s}-\frac{1}{s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{4}^{a}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-4s}}{s}-\frac{1}{s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{{e}^{-st}}{s})|}_{4}^{a} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-4s}}{s}-\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{-sa}-{e}^{-4s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-4s}}{s}-\frac{1}{s}-\frac{1}{s}(0-{e}^{-4s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-4s}}{s}-\frac{1}{s}+\frac{{e}^{-4s}}{s} \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{-4s}}{s}-\frac{1}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

valid for $s>0.$

questions.problem:
Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s)=L{f(t)},$ where $f(t)=u(t-3)$ and $u$ is the unit step function.

$F(s)=L{f(t)}=$
{{field-1}},
valid for $s\,$

questions.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the unit step function is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<0 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise function 

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t-3)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<3 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 3\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }u(t-3){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}0\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }1\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this improper integral diverges if $s\le 0.$

For $s>0,$ we calculate this integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{3}^{a}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{{e}^{-st}}{s})|}_{3}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{1}{s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{-sa}-{e}^{-3s}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{s}(0-{e}^{-3s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-3s}}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
L{f(t)}=\frac{{e}^{-3s}}{s},\,s>0.
$$

questions.problem:
Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s)=L{f(t)},$ where $f(t)$ is given by 

$$
f(t)={\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t},\, & t\le 1 \\ 1\, & t>1.\end{aligned}
$$

$\,F(s)=L{f(t)}=$ {{field-1}},
valid for {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise function 

$$
f(t)={\begin{aligned}{e}^{5t},\, & t\le 1 \\ 1\, & t>1\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{5t}\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }1\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{5t-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{(5-s)t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the improper integral diverges if $s\le 0.$

For $s>0,$ we calculate our Laplace transform as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{(5-s)t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{5-s}{[{e}^{(5-s)t}]}_{0}^{1}+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{e}^{(5-s)}-1}{5-s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{e}^{(5-s)}-1}{5-s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{-{e}^{-st}}{s})|}_{1}^{a} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{(5-s)}-1}{5-s}-\frac{1}{s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{-as}-{e}^{-s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{(5-s)}-1}{5-s}-\frac{1}{s}\cdot (0-{e}^{-s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{(5-s)}-1}{5-s}+\frac{{e}^{-s}}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

valid for $s>0.$

questions.problem:
Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s)=L{f(t)},$ where $f(t)$ is given by 

$$
f(t)={\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t},\, & t\le 2 \\ 2\, & t>2.\end{aligned}
$$

$\,F(s)=L{f(t)}=$ {{field-1}},
valid for {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise function 

$$
f(t)={\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t},\, & t\le 2 \\ 2\, & t>2\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{3t}\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{2}^{\infty }2\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{3t-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{2}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{(3-s)t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{2}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the improper integral diverges if $s\le 0.$

For $s>0,$ we calculate our Laplace transform as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{e}^{(3-s)t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{2}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{3-s}{[{e}^{(3-s)t}]}_{0}^{2}+{\int }_{2}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2(3-s)}-1}{3-s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{2}^{a}2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2(3-s)}-1}{3-s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{-2{e}^{-st}}{s})|}_{2}^{a} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2(3-s)}-1}{3-s}-\frac{2}{s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{-as}-{e}^{-2s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2(3-s)}-1}{3-s}-\frac{2}{s}\cdot (0-{e}^{-2s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2(3-s)}-1}{3-s}+\frac{2{e}^{-2s}}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

valid for $s>0.$

questions.problem:
Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s)=L{f(t)},$ where $f(t)$ is given by 

$$
f(t)={\begin{aligned}3,\, & t\le 5 \\ {e}^{3t}\, & t>5.\end{aligned}
$$

$\,F(s)=L{f(t)}=$ {{field-1}},
valid for {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise function 

$$
f(t)={\begin{aligned}3,\, & t\le 5 \\ {e}^{3t}\, & t>5\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}3\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{5}^{\infty }{e}^{3t}\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}3\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{5}^{\infty }{e}^{3t-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{5}3{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{5}^{\infty }{e}^{(3-s)t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the improper integral diverges if $s\le 3.$

For $s>3,$ we calculate our Laplace transform as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{5}3{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{5}^{\infty }{e}^{(3-s)t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{3}{s}{[{e}^{-st}]}_{0}^{5}+{\int }_{5}^{\infty }{e}^{(3-s)t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{3}{s}-\frac{3{e}^{-5s}}{s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{5}^{a}{e}^{(3-s)t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{3}{s}-\frac{3{e}^{-5s}}{s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{{e}^{(3-s)t}}{3-s})|}_{5}^{a} \\  & =\frac{3}{s}-\frac{3{e}^{-5s}}{s}+\frac{1}{3-s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{(3-s)a}-{e}^{5(3-s)}) \\  & =\frac{3}{s}-\frac{3{e}^{-5s}}{s}+\frac{1}{3-s}\cdot (0-{e}^{5(3-s)}) \\  & =\frac{3}{s}-\frac{3{e}^{-5s}}{s}+\frac{{e}^{5(3-s)}}{s-3}\end{aligned}
$$

valid for $s>3.$

questions.problem:
Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s)=L{f(t)},$ where $f(t)$ is given by 

$$
f(t)={\begin{aligned}{e}^{t},\, & t\le 4 \\ 2\, & t>4.\end{aligned}
$$

$\,F(s)=L{f(t)}=$ {{field-1}},
valid for {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise function 

$$
f(t)={\begin{aligned}{e}^{t},\, & t\le 4 \\ 2\, & t>4\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{4}^{\infty }2\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{e}^{t-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{4}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{e}^{(1-s)t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{4}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the improper integral diverges if $s\le 0.$

For $s>0,$ we calculate our Laplace transform as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{e}^{(1-s)t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{4}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{1-s}{[{e}^{(1-s)t}]}_{0}^{4}+{\int }_{4}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{e}^{4(1-s)}-1}{1-s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{4}^{a}2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{e}^{4(1-s)}-1}{1-s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{-2{e}^{-st}}{s})|}_{4}^{a} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{4(1-s)}-1}{1-s}-\frac{2}{s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{-as}-{e}^{-4s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{4(1-s)}-1}{1-s}-\frac{2}{s}\cdot (0-{e}^{-4s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{4(1-s)}-1}{1-s}+\frac{2{e}^{-4s}}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

valid for $s>0.$

questions.problem:
Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s)=L{f(t)},$ where $f(t)$ is given by 

$$
f(t)={\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t},\, & t\le 1 \\ 4\, & t>1.\end{aligned}
$$

$\,F(s)=L{f(t)}=$ {{field-1}},
valid for {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise function 

$$
f(t)={\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t},\, & t\le 1 \\ 4\, & t>1\end{aligned}
$$

we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{-3t}\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }4\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{-3t-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }4\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{-(3+s)t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }4{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the improper integral diverges if $s\le 0.$

For $s>0,$ we calculate our Laplace transform as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{-(3+s)t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }4{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{-(3+s)}{[{e}^{-(3+s)t}]}_{0}^{1}+{\int }_{1}^{\infty }4{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{-(3+s)}}{3+s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{1}^{a}4{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{-(3+s)}}{3+s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{-4{e}^{-st}}{s})|}_{1}^{a} \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{-(3+s)}}{3+s}-\frac{4}{s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{-as}-{e}^{-s}) \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{-(3+s)}}{3+s}-\frac{4}{s}\cdot (0-{e}^{-s}) \\  & =\frac{1-{e}^{-(3+s)}}{3+s}+\frac{4{e}^{-s}}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

valid for $s>0.$

canonical_examples.problem: Use the definition of Laplace transforms to calculate $F(s) = \mathcal L\{f(t)\}$ for $f(t) = u(t - 2) + u(t-6),$ where $u$ is the unit step function.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We apply the definition of the Laplace transform:

$$
\begin{aligned}L{f(t)} & =F(s)={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the unit step function is defined as

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t)={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<0 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 0.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, for the piecewise functions $u(t-2)$ and $u(t-6),$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t-2) & ={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<2 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 2\end{aligned} \\ u(t-6) & ={\begin{aligned}0,\, & t<6 \\ 1,\, & t\ge 6.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14043349/assets/6ddb2983dec1f3221778a336bb6ef3cce3138476b67d64334ab6660184a79f95.png)

So, for our Laplace transform, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}0\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{2}^{6}1\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{6}^{\infty }2\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{6}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{6}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the second integral diverges for $s \leq 0.$

For $s > 0,$ we calculate our Laplace transform as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{2}^{6}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{6}^{\infty }2{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{2}^{6}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{6}^{a}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={[-\frac{{e}^{-st}}{s}]}_{2}^{6}+2{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(-\frac{{e}^{-st}}{s})|}_{6}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{-6s}}{s}+\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s}-\frac{2}{s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{-sa}-{e}^{-6s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s}-\frac{{e}^{-6s}}{s}-\frac{2}{s}(0-{e}^{-6s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s}-\frac{{e}^{-6s}}{s}+\frac{2{e}^{-6s}}{s} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-2s}}{s}+\frac{{e}^{-6s}}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} =\dfrac{e^{-2s}}{s} +\dfrac{e^{-6s}}{s}, 
\qquad 
s > 0.
$$

\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{\infty }f(t){e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{2t}\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }1\cdot {e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{2t-st}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{(2-s)t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the improper integral diverges if $s \leq 0.$

For $s > 0,$ we calculate our Laplace transform as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}F(s) & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{e}^{(2-s)t}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2-s}{[{e}^{(2-s)t}]}_{0}^{3}+{\int }_{3}^{\infty }{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3(2-s)}-1}{2-s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{3}^{a}{e}^{-st}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3(2-s)}-1}{2-s}+{lim}_{a\to \infty }{(\frac{-{e}^{-st}}{s})|}_{3}^{a} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3(2-s)}-1}{2-s}-\frac{1}{s}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }({e}^{-as}-{e}^{-3s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3(2-s)}-1}{2-s}-\frac{1}{s}\cdot (0-{e}^{-3s}) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{3(2-s)}-1}{2-s}+\frac{{e}^{-3s}}{s}\end{aligned}
$$

valid for $s > 0.$
